summary: Computing constrained traffic engineering paths across multiple domains is a key requirement. This experimental RFC defines domain subobjects for PCEP, letting a domain such as an IGP area or autonomous system be named in path computation.

plainLanguage.summary: Path computation lets a network's control software work out a route across a network instead of each router working it out alone. This RFC adds a way to say, inside such a request, which parts of the network the route must cross or must avoid, naming whole areas and whole autonomous systems.

subtitle: New route-object elements that let path computation name whole domains, such as IGP areas and autonomous systems, to cross or avoid.

tldr.problem: Both per-domain and backward-recursive path computation assume that the sequence of domains to be crossed is already known, either fixed by the operator or discovered separately.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three new subobjects, a 4-byte AS number, an OSPF area ID and an IS-IS area ID, that can be carried in the Include, Exclude and Explicit Route objects of PCEP messages.
tldr.outcome: A PCE reading such an object can tell which autonomous system or area it is in and which PCE to hand the request to next, so a domain sequence can be carried inside the path computation request itself.

facts.label: New IRO and XRO subobject types
facts.value: 5 (4-byte AS number), 6 (OSPF Area ID), 7 (IS-IS Area ID)

facts.label: IS-IS area subobject length
facts.value: At least 8 octets, a multiple of 4

facts.label: X bit
facts.value: 0 means MUST exclude, 1 means SHOULD avoid

today: RFC 7897 is an Experimental RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The document describes a two-year experiment, after which its authors planned to check how widely it had been implemented and deployed before considering a move to the Standards Track.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) may be used to compute end-to-end paths across multi-domain environments using a per-domain path computation technique (RFC 5152). The Backward-Recursive PCE-Based Computation (BRPC) mechanism (RFC 5441) also defines a PCE-based procedure to compute an inter-domain constrained path for (G)MPLS TE LSPs.

However, both the per-domain and the BRPC technique assume that the sequence of domains to be crossed from source to destination is known, and is either fixed by the network operator or obtained by other means. For inter-domain point-to-multipoint tree computation, it is assumed that the domain tree is known in advance. The list of domains, called the domain sequence, is therefore usually a constraint on an inter-domain path computation procedure.

RFC 5440 defines the Include Route Object (IRO) and the Explicit Route Object (ERO), and RFC 5521 defines the Exclude Route Object (XRO) and the Explicit Exclusion Route subobject (EXRS). The use of an Autonomous System as an abstract node representing a domain is defined in RFC 3209. This document specifies new subobjects to include or exclude domains, including an IGP area or an AS with a 4-byte AS number as per RFC 6793. The domain identifier may also simply act as a delimiter to say where a domain boundary starts and ends.
sections.plainLanguage: Path computation lets a network's control software work out a route across a network instead of each router working it out alone. This RFC adds a way to say, inside such a request, which parts of the network the route must cross or must avoid, naming whole areas and whole autonomous systems.

sections.title: Scope of the Experiment
sections.content:
The procedures described in the document are experimental. The experiment is intended to enable research into the use of the domain sequence at PCEs for inter-domain paths, and the document specifies the new domain subobjects and how they combine with existing subobjects to represent a domain sequence.

The experiment will end two years after the RFC is published. At that point the authors will attempt to determine how widely this has been implemented and deployed.

The document does not change the procedures for handling existing subobjects in PCEP. The new subobjects will not be understood by legacy implementations, and a legacy implementation that receives one it does not understand will behave according to the rules for a malformed object in RFC 5440. The experiment is therefore assumed to be conducted only when both the PCE and the Path Computation Client (PCC) form part of it. A PCC or PCE may also have peers that are not part of the experiment, and because no capabilities exchange identifies which nodes can use these extensions, manual configuration should be used to determine which peerings take part.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a trial. An old device that meets one of the new subobjects will treat the message as malformed and refuse it, so only devices taking part in the trial should exchange these messages.

sections.title: Domains, Domain Sequences and Route Objects
sections.content:
RFC 4655 defines a domain as any collection of network elements within a common sphere of address management or path computational responsibility. Examples of domains include an IGP area and an AS. Each AS can be made of several IGP areas. To encode a domain sequence, a domain has to be uniquely identified, and it can be identified by an area ID, an AS number, or both.

A domain sequence is an ordered sequence of domains traversed to reach the destination domain. It can be applied as a constraint carried in a path computation request, and it can also be the result of a path computation: in the Hierarchical PCE model (RFC 6805), a parent PCE can send the domain sequence back as a result in a path computation reply. In a point-to-point path the domains appear in the order they are crossed; in a point-to-multipoint path the domain tree is represented as a list of domain sequences.

A domain sequence is made up of one or more of: AS number, area ID, boundary node ID, and inter-AS link address. These are encoded in the new subobjects defined here as well as in existing subobjects. A domain sequence can therefore be used by a PCE to discover or select the next PCE in a collaborative computation, by a parent PCE to return the sequence when it is unknown, by a PCC or PCE to constrain which domains are expanded or excluded, and by a PCE in the per-domain model to identify the next domain.

The domain sequence appears in PCEP messages in four places. The Include Route Object specifies a set of network elements to be traversed to reach the destination. The Exclude Route Object specifies abstract nodes to be excluded from the whole path. The Explicit Exclusion Route subobject sits inside the IRO and excludes abstract nodes between a specific pair of nodes. The Explicit Route Object specifies a computed path, so a parent PCE can return the domain sequence as a result in a path computation reply.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain is a part of the network with its own address management or its own path calculations, such as one area inside a routing domain. The new subobjects name those parts one after another, in the order the path crosses them.

sections.title: The New Domain Subobjects
sections.content:
Some subobjects were already defined in RFC 3209, RFC 3473, RFC 3477 and RFC 4874, but new subobjects related to the domain sequence are needed. The document extends the support for 4-byte AS numbers and IGP areas, adding three subobject types to both the IRO Subobjects and the XRO Subobjects registries: value 5 for a 4-byte AS number, value 6 for an OSPF Area ID and value 7 for an IS-IS Area ID. Identical subobjects are carried in RSVP-TE messages as defined in RFC 7898.

The 4-byte AS number subobject has the L bit as its first bit, the Type field set to 5, a Length of 8 octets, 2 octets of Reserved that are zero at transmission and ignored at receipt, and the 4-byte AS number. If 2-byte AS numbers are in use, the low-order bits, 16 through 31, MUST be used and the high-order bits, 0 through 15, MUST be set to zero.

Because the length and format of an Area ID differs between OSPF and IS-IS, two separate subobjects are defined. The OSPF Area ID subobject has Type 6, a Length of 8 octets and a 4-byte OSPF area number. The IS-IS Area ID subobject has Type 7, a variable Length that MUST be at least 8 and MUST be a multiple of 4, an Area-Len octet holding the length of the real, unpadded IS-IS area identifier, with valid values from 1 to 13 inclusive, and the variable-length IS-IS area identifier padded with trailing zeroes to a 4-byte boundary.

In the XRO the same subobjects appear with an X bit instead of the L bit. A value of 0 means the named AS or area MUST be excluded from the computed path. A value of 1 means it SHOULD be avoided, but MAY be included subject to PCE policy and the absence of a viable path that meets the other constraints. All other fields are consistent with the IRO definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new small blocks of data are added to the messages: one naming an autonomous system by its 4-byte number, one naming an OSPF area, and one naming an IS-IS area. In an exclusion list, a single bit decides whether the named area is forbidden or merely discouraged.

sections.title: How a PCE Reads an Include Route Object
sections.content:
When a PCE parses an IRO, it interprets each subobject according to the AS number associated with the preceding subobject, which the document calls the current AS. The current AS is initialized to the AS number of the PCC. Encountering an AS subobject updates the current AS. Encountering an area subobject means the area belongs to the current AS. Encountering a globally routable IP address updates the current AS to the AS that owns that address, although the document does not define how the PCE learns which AS owns an address. A non-globally-routable IP address and an unnumbered link are assumed to belong to the current AS.

The same parsing tracks a current area, initialized to the area ID of the PCC. If the current AS changes, the current area is reset and must be determined again by a current or subsequent subobject. An area subobject updates the current area. An IP address belonging to a different area updates the current area to that area, and so does an unnumbered link belonging to a different area. Otherwise the subobject is assumed to belong to the current area. The document advises that a PCC should use AS and area subobjects while building the domain sequence, and avoid other mechanisms that would change the current AS and current area.

Where the current PCE is not responsible for path computation in the current AS or area, it selects the next PCE in the domain sequence based on the current AS and area. The mapping between domains and responsible PCEs is not defined in the document; it is assumed that a PCE needing a next PCE from a domain sequence can obtain it, for example by administrative configuration or discovery.

Other cases are covered elsewhere in the document. A single PCE may be responsible for several domains, for example a PCE function deployed on an ABR, and can handle those domains internally. The EXRS can carry any of the XRO subobjects, but the scope of the exclusion is limited to the single hop between the previous and subsequent elements in the IRO, and the EXRS does not change the current AS or current area. The ERO can carry the new subobjects to specify an abstract node, so an explicitly routed LSP can be given as a sequence of domains, and the ERO in a reply from a parent PCE can be used in per-domain path computation or BRPC.
sections.plainLanguage: As the PCE walks through the list, it keeps track of which autonomous system it has reached and which area inside it. When it reaches a domain it does not serve itself, it hands the request to the PCE that does.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol extensions do not substantially change the nature of PCEP, so the security considerations of RFC 5440 apply unchanged, and further considerations for the use of PCEP over TCP are set out in RFC 6952. The security considerations of the mechanisms that use domain sequences, such as RFC 5152, RFC 5441, RFC 6805 and RFC 7334, remain unchanged by the new subobjects.

The new subobjects do allow finer and more specific control of the path computed by cooperating PCEs. That control increases the risk if a PCEP message is intercepted, modified or spoofed, because it lets an attacker exert control over the path the PCE will compute, or make the path computation impossible. Implementations should therefore conform to the relevant security requirements of RFC 5440: securing PCEP session messages using TCP security techniques, and considering the additional security of TCP-AO (RFC 5925) or TLS; authenticating PCEP messages so they are intact and come from an authorized node; and protecting the PCE and PCC against TCP denial-of-service attacks. In inter-AS scenarios, attacks may be particularly significant, with commercial as well as service-level implications.

The document also notes that domain sequences give the operator the ability to route around vulnerable parts of the network, and may be used to increase overall network security.
sections.plainLanguage: Because these subobjects let a request name exactly which parts of the network a path must use, an attacker who could alter the message has more control than before. The document therefore repeats the existing requirements for protecting PCEP sessions and authenticating messages.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: Attribute bit of the subobject; its use in an IRO is defined in RFC 7896.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the subobject, in bytes.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero at transmission; ignored at receipt.

fields.name: AS Number
fields.desc: The 4-byte AS number. With 2-byte AS numbers, bits 16 through 31 carry the number and bits 0 through 15 are zero.

messages.label: PCReq WITH IRO
messages.note: The client lists the domains to cross, using the new AS and area subobjects.

messages.label: FORWARDED REQUEST
messages.note: When the current PCE does not serve the current AS or area, it selects the next PCE in the domain sequence and forwards the request.

messages.label: PCRep
messages.note: The reply carries the computed path, and may carry the domain sequence in an ERO.
